decks.domain: Required vehicle equipment, lights, tires and glass

cards.front: What should you check before driving a vehicle on public roads?
cards.back: Before driving on public roads, make sure the vehicle is fully equipped and in good condition, read the owner's manual, and regularly check the lights, wipers, horn and tires.

cards.front: What should you do when you first get into the vehicle?
cards.back: When you get in, adjust your seat and mirrors, seat passengers where they do not block your view or interfere with driving, and buckle up and have every passenger do the same.

cards.front: How many separate brake systems must every car and truck have?
cards.back: Every car and truck must have at least two separate brake systems, such as the foot brake and the parking or emergency brake.

cards.front: What bumpers do passenger cars, pickups and vans need?
cards.back: Private passenger vehicles must have front and rear bumpers, while pickup trucks and vans need a front bumper plus either a rear bumper or reflectors.

cards.front: May a pickup or van use reflectors instead of a rear bumper?
cards.back: A private passenger car needs bumpers front and rear, but a pickup or van may use reflectors in place of a rear bumper as long as it has a front bumper.

cards.front: What sound devices may an ordinary vehicle have?
cards.back: A vehicle must have a working horn, and bells, sirens and whistles are reserved for emergency vehicles.

cards.front: When should you use your horn?
cards.back: Use the horn to avoid a crash, never needlessly or to announce that you have arrived.

cards.front: Which items appear on the required equipment list?
cards.back: The required-equipment diagram lists wipers, safety glass, a rearview mirror, horn, plates with a plate light, two ways to brake, high and low beam headlights, turn signals, bumpers, seat belts, a muffler, and a red taillight with red reflectors and a stop light.

decks.domain: Required vehicle equipment, lights, tires and glass

cards.front: What headlights and taillights must every motor vehicle except a motorcycle have?
cards.back: Every motor vehicle except a motorcycle needs two white headlights that work on both high and low beam and red taillights that light up when the brake pedal is pressed.
cards.memory_hook: Two white, both beams, red brakes

cards.front: How far ahead must high beams light up objects on the road?
cards.back: High beams must light up objects on the road at least three hundred fifty feet ahead.

cards.front: Why must damaged headlights be replaced?
cards.back: Damaged headlights must be replaced, because a cracked lens lets in moisture and dust that cut light output and add glare for other drivers.

cards.front: How much light can dirty headlights lose?
cards.back: Dirty headlights can cut light output by as much as seventy-five percent, so clean them as often as the windshield.

cards.front: How often should headlight aim be inspected?
cards.back: Have the headlights inspected at least once a year to make sure they are aimed correctly.

cards.front: What do daytime running lights do, and what do they not turn on?
cards.back: Daytime running lights may switch on automatically to make a vehicle more visible, but taillights and parking lights do not come on automatically.

cards.front: When must your headlights be on?
cards.back: Headlights go on at sunset and stay on until sunrise, and also in rain, snow, hail, sleet or fog or whenever you cannot see the road at least five hundred feet ahead.

cards.front: Which other lights must work besides headlights and taillights?
cards.back: A white light must light the rear license plate so it can be seen at night, and every turn signal light on the vehicle must work.

cards.front: Which two headlight distances must you keep apart?
cards.back: Two different distances apply to headlights: high beams must show objects at least three hundred fifty feet ahead, while headlights must be on any time you cannot see the road for at least five hundred feet.
cards.memory_hook: Three fifty reach, five hundred see

cards.front: Do daytime running lights mean you can skip switching on headlights at sunset?
cards.back: Daytime running lights can turn on by themselves, but taillights and parking lights never do, so at sunset you still switch on your headlights.

decks.module: Restricted lights, mufflers, mirrors and belts
decks.domain: Required vehicle equipment, lights, tires and glass

cards.front: Which vehicles may use blue lights?
cards.back: Blue lights are limited to snowplows, road maintenance equipment and authorized emergency vehicles.

cards.front: Which vehicles may use flashing lights?
cards.back: Flashing lights are limited to tow trucks, school buses, farm equipment, service vehicles, road maintenance equipment and authorized emergency vehicles.

cards.front: Which vehicles may use strobe lamps?
cards.back: Strobe lamps are limited to school buses, snow removal equipment and rural mail carrier vehicles.

cards.front: May a tow truck use blue lights?
cards.back: Blue lights belong only to snowplows, road maintenance equipment and emergency vehicles, while tow trucks, service vehicles and farm equipment may show flashing lights but not blue ones.

cards.front: Which vehicle may use strobes but is not on the flashing-light list?
cards.back: School buses may use both flashing lights and strobe lamps, and rural mail carrier vehicles may use strobe lamps but are not on the flashing-light list.

cards.front: Why does every vehicle need a muffler, and what should you check it for?
cards.back: Every motor vehicle needs a muffler to prevent sudden or prolonged loud noise such as popping or crackling, and the muffler should be checked regularly for carbon monoxide leaks.

cards.front: Which mirrors do passenger vehicles and hauling pickups need?
cards.back: Passenger vehicles need rearview mirrors, and a vehicle with no view through a rear window, such as a rental moving truck, or a pickup used for hauling needs an extra side mirror.

cards.front: When is an extra side mirror needed?
cards.back: Every passenger vehicle needs a rearview mirror, and a hauling pickup or a vehicle with no view through the rear window needs an extra side mirror as well.

cards.front: Who must wear seat belts in Minnesota vehicles?
cards.back: Minnesota requires seat belts in all vehicles and requires everyone to wear them, and belts should be kept clean and in good condition for all occupants.

cards.front: Can airbags keep you from being thrown out of a vehicle?
cards.back: Airbags work together with seat belts but do not keep occupants from being thrown out, and a cluttered dashboard can turn objects into hazards when airbags inflate.

decks.domain: Required vehicle equipment, lights, tires and glass

cards.front: What should you look for when inspecting your tires?
cards.back: Look over your tires often for bulges, punctures, bald spots, cuts, cracks or uneven wear, and carry a good spare whose pressure you check often.

cards.front: How does tire grip on gravel or dirt compare with pavement?
cards.back: Tires grip gravel or dirt roads less well than concrete or asphalt.

cards.front: Where do you find the recommended tire pressure?
cards.back: The recommended tire pressure is on a sticker inside the driver's door or in the owner's manual, not the number printed on the tire sidewall.

cards.front: When should you check tire pressure?
cards.back: Check tire pressure before driving or at least three hours after driving, then add or release air until the gauge matches the recommended number.
cards.memory_hook: Check cold or wait three hours

cards.front: Is the number on the tire sidewall the pressure to aim for?
cards.back: The tire pressure to aim for is the one on the driver's door sticker or in the owner's manual, while the sidewall number is not the target.

cards.front: Should you check tire pressure right after a drive?
cards.back: Tire pressure is checked either before you drive or only once at least three hours have passed since driving, not right after a trip.

cards.front: When is a tire's tread illegally shallow?
cards.back: A tire is illegal when its tread is less than one-sixteenth of an inch deep.

cards.front: How does the penny test show a tire is legal?
cards.back: In the penny test you place Lincoln's head into the shallowest tread groove, and if the tread covers any part of his head the tire is legal and safe.

cards.front: How do the legal tread limit and the penny test relate?
cards.back: The legal tread limit is one-sixteenth of an inch, and the penny test passes only when tread covers part of Lincoln's head.

decks.domain: Required vehicle equipment, lights, tires and glass

cards.front: What may not block the view through your windshield and windows?
cards.back: The view through the windshield and windows must not be blocked by cracks, discoloration, steam, frost, ice or snow, and nothing may hang between the driver and the windshield.

cards.front: What may be placed on or near the windshield?
cards.back: Stickers allowed by state law, such as park stickers, safety inspection stickers and toll devices, may go on the windshield, navigation units may mount near its bottom, and driver monitoring equipment may sit just behind, above or below the rearview mirror.

cards.front: May you hang an object between yourself and the windshield?
cards.back: Toll devices and park or inspection stickers allowed by state law may go on the windshield, but objects may not hang between the driver and the windshield.

cards.front: What materials may not be used on a windshield?
cards.back: A windshield may not be made of, covered with or treated with any material that makes it more reflective or lets less light through.

cards.front: What labeling must side or rear window tint carry?
cards.back: Side or rear window tint applied after Aug. one, nineteen eighty-five must be labeled with the percentage of light it transmits and reflects.

cards.front: Where is dark or highly reflective tint allowed?
cards.back: Tint that transmits less than fifty percent or reflects more than twenty percent of light is allowed only on a pickup's rear window or on the rear and side windows of a van, limousine or funeral home vehicle.

cards.front: Is dark tint ever allowed on the windshield?
cards.back: Dark tint that lets through less than fifty percent of light or reflects more than twenty percent is limited to pickup rear windows and to the rear and side windows of vans, limousines and funeral home vehicles, never the windshield.

cards.front: What must a vehicle with a glass windshield have to keep the view clear?
cards.back: A vehicle with a glass windshield must have working wipers, and defrosters are needed to keep the windshield and windows free of steam and frost.

cards.front: Why do passenger vehicles need fenders or wheel guards?
cards.back: Passenger vehicles need fenders or other wheel guards so the tires do not throw water, dirt and debris into the air.

decks.domain: Required vehicle equipment, lights, tires and glass

cards.front: What vehicle care helps save fuel?
cards.back: Save fuel by keeping the engine tuned, the tires properly inflated and the recommended grade of motor oil in the engine.

cards.front: Which driving habits save fuel?
cards.back: Drive efficiently by combining errands, avoiding speeding, hard acceleration and sudden braking, obeying the speed limit, removing heavy items you do not need, and using cruise control and overdrive on the highway.

cards.front: Which travel choices save fuel?
cards.back: Public transportation, carpools, ridesharing, biking or walking are recommended whenever possible to save fuel.

recap_hooks.text: Check your vehicle and buckle everyone in before driving, and make sure it has two separate brake systems and the right bumpers.
Use the horn only to avoid a crash; sirens and bells belong to emergency vehicles.
High beams must reach three hundred fifty feet, and headlights go on from sunset to sunrise, in bad weather or when you cannot see five hundred feet.
Daytime running lights do not turn on taillights, so switch on your headlights yourself.

recaps.module: Restricted lights, mufflers, mirrors and belts

recap_hooks.text: Blue lights are for plows, road maintenance and emergency vehicles, flashing lights for a longer list including tow trucks, and strobes for school buses, snow removal and mail carriers.
Everyone must wear a seat belt, and airbags help but cannot keep you in the vehicle.
Use the pressure on the door sticker or in the owner's manual, checked before driving or three hours after.
Tread under one-sixteenth of an inch is illegal, and the penny test passes when tread covers part of Lincoln's head.
Keep the glass clear and hang nothing in front of you, though legal stickers and toll devices may go on the windshield.
Dark or highly reflective tint is limited to certain rear and side windows, never the windshield.
Save fuel with a tuned engine, inflated tires, smooth driving, combined errands and shared or active travel.

merges.justification: The accepted spoken wording of sec04-F25 contains the bare unit abbreviation PSI, which fails the spoken-form rule and cannot be reworded on a card back; its point (tires slowly lose pressure, so check often) is carried by the sec04-F27 pressure-check card and its narration, which cite both facts.
